subject: chemical
audience: FE Chemical candidates and chemical engineering students
title: The Liquid Mixture That Started Boiling at 64 kPa
featured_title: THE LIQUID MIXTURE THAT STARTED BOILING AT 64 KPA

presentation.challenge: A binary liquid did not boil when total pressure equaled either pure-component vapor pressure. Its bubble pressure was the composition-weighted sum.

practice.primary_question: How does Raoult's law determine the bubble pressure of an ideal binary liquid mixture?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Averaging pure-component vapor pressures directly instead of weighting them by liquid composition.

case_dna.target_misconception: The bubble pressure of a binary ideal liquid is just the arithmetic average of the two pure-component saturation pressures.
case_dna.why_plausible: There are two components, so a simple average can look reasonable when composition is overlooked.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With xA=0.40, PsatA=100 kPa, xB=0.60, and PsatB=40 kPa, Pbubble=xA PsatA+xB PsatB=64 kPa.
case_dna.corrected_model: For an ideal liquid mixture, use Raoult's law: yiP=xiPsat_i and Pbubble=sum(xiPsat_i).

problem_statement: An ideal binary liquid at a fixed temperature contains 40 mol% component A and 60 mol% component B. At this temperature, the pure-component saturation pressures are 100 kPa for A and 40 kPa for B. A calculation averages the two values and predicts a 70 kPa bubble pressure. Determine the correct bubble pressure and the vapor-phase mole fraction of A at incipient boiling.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The pure-component pressures were known. Composition still mattered.
gates.prompt: How should each saturation pressure contribute to total bubble pressure?

options.label: Use P=sum(xi Psat,i)
options.reason: Raoult's law weights each saturation pressure by its liquid mole fraction.

options.label: Use (100+40)/2=70 kPa
options.reason: That ignores the actual liquid composition.

options.label: Use only the larger saturation pressure, 100 kPa
options.reason: Both components contribute partial pressure at the bubble point.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the bubble pressure
gates.prompt: What total pressure in kPa marks incipient boiling?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Lower the system pressure
gates.result: The liquid begins to boil at 64 kPa.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the bubble pressure
gates.hint: Weight each pure-component vapor pressure by its liquid mole fraction.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Partial pressures add to the bubble pressure

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the phase-equilibrium note
report: C3. The bubble pressure is their arithmetic average, 70 kPa.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: The calculation ignores liquid mole fractions.

evidence_choices.label: 0.40(100)+0.60(40)=64 kPa
evidence_choices.reason: This is the ideal-mixture bubble-pressure relation.

correction.template: The bubble pressure is {pressure} kPa and the first vapor has yA={yA}.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Raise the bubble pressure at the same temperature
gates.constraint: Keep the same two ideal components and temperature.

options.label: Increase the liquid mole fraction of A
options.reason: A has the larger saturation pressure, so increasing xA raises the composition-weighted total.

options.label: Increase the liquid mole fraction of B
options.reason: B has the lower saturation pressure, so this lowers the bubble pressure.

options.label: Ignore composition and use the arithmetic mean
options.reason: That does not represent Raoult's law.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply ideal-mixture bubble pressure
gates.prompt: For xA=0.50, Psat,A=80 kPa and Psat,B=20 kPa, what is the bubble pressure?

options.label: 30 kPa
options.reason: That is not the weighted sum.

gates.explanation: For an ideal binary mixture, bubble pressure is the sum of xiPsat,i.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the VLE model
gates.confirmation: I confirm that ideal-mixture bubble pressure depends on both saturation pressures and liquid composition.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Pure-component vapor pressures were averaged without composition weighting.

seo.seo_title: Raoult's Law Bubble Pressure: Why the Mixture Boils at 64 kPa | FE E-064
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Chemical Case E-064: an ideal 40/60 binary liquid with saturation pressures 100 and 40 kPa has a 64 kPa bubble pressure.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Chemical Raoult law bubble pressure
seo.excerpt: Bubble pressure is a composition-weighted sum, not a simple average of pure-component vapor pressures.
seo.direct_answer: For an ideal binary liquid, Pbubble=sum(xiPsat,i). With xA=0.40, Psat,A=100 kPa, xB=0.60, and Psat,B=40 kPa, Pbubble=64 kPa. The first vapor has yA=40/64=0.625.

faqs.q: How do you calculate ideal-mixture bubble pressure?
faqs.a: Use the sum of liquid mole fraction times saturation pressure for each component.

faqs.q: What is yA at this bubble point?
